newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST - Australian General News - Jan 16.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Australian General News - Jan 16.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

An index prepared by Westpac Banking Corp and the Melbourne Institute of Applied Economic and Social Research rose four per cent during January. The index, the main measure of consumer confidence in Australia, offsets a fall of seven per cent during Deceber which accompanied reports of poor performances from most retailers over Christmas. Page 3.

Australian Conservation Foundation spokesman Mike Krockenberger said last night the ACF was extremely disappointed in the Federal Government's cut in funding from A$187,000 to A$110,000 for 1996-97. The cuts, announced by Federal Environment Minister Robrt Hill, accompanied a retention of total funding for voluntary conservation groups at around the same level as the former Labor Government. Page 3.

Western Australia Premier Richard Court says Australia must develop a taxation regime comparable to those in Singapore or Hong Kong if it wishes to remain competitive into the next century. Court says Australia's comparatively narrow, income-based system is putting pressure on spending programs in health, housing, aged services and higher education. Page 3.

The Queensland Government may be in more trouble over the native title issue as a senior Government source indicated the Government did not obtain formal, written Crown Law advice when it decided to freeze dealings on most leasehold property in the State.Page 5.
THE AUSTRALIAN

In controversial remarks expected to upset the academia, Rod West, the chairman of the Federal Government's new higher education review committee, said yesterday universities should not offer vocational courses such as Diplomas of Education, but should intead concentrate on "creative thinking" and "inspirational teaching". West will head the seven-person committee which has been given a wide brief to draw up a blueprint for the A$5 billion higher education sector over the next two decades. Page 1.

Acting Prime Minister Tim Fischer yesterday hardened his stance on native title by pointing out Parliament's supremacy over the High Court and problems with its Wik decision. Fischer said the Federal Government and Parliament had certain responsibilitiesand obligations apart from what the High Court may determine. Page 1.

Analyst and business forecaster Phil Ruthven says there are a number of trends in the lifestyle of Australians that could cause trouble for retailers. The social and demographic changes in the Australian consumer leaves it almost unrecognisable from a deade or so ago, with spending patterns changing and many businesses struggling as a result. Page 3.

Federal Liberal backbencher and chairman of the parliamentary committee into the National Crime Authority, John Bradford, said yesterday the Federal Government's fight against illegal drugs had little co-ordination and urgency. Bradford's comments followa report by the Australian Bureau of Criminal Intelligence that shows a rise in drug use despite huge increases in arrests for drug-related crimes. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

A peace deal between Kerry Packer and Rupert Murdoch is imminent, as negotiators for News Corporation and the Nine Network thrash out a deal for the television rights to Super League. An announcement, expected tomorrow, should see Nine get the rights to televise Monday Night football. Page 1.

In a move to make Asia the top of the international agenda for 1997, Prime Minister John Howard is planning a diplomatic trip through key Asian capitals in April that aims to boost Australia's regional interests, including a bid for a A$3 billion defence eal with Malaysia that has run into trouble. Page 1.

The Department of Employment, Education, Training and Youth Affairs has warned the results of recent surveys conducted by the Department do not foreshadow any improvement in job growth in the near future, and there are indications of low consumer sentimen and a decline in housing finance commitments that have reinforced the bleak outlook for the economy. Page 3.

As the New South Wales Government awaits the report from a review of the school starting age for children, children entering kindergarten this year will be monitored, following concerns that children would turn six in the year they begin school. A proposal that would copy the current system in Victoria would see children born in May, June and July having to start school in the year they turned six rather than five. Page 3.
THE AGE

As Victorian students await Monday's first round of enrolment offers, State universities look set to reject more school leavers with low TERs in an attempt to shore up their entrance scores and protect their reputation. To fill the void, course quotas are likely to be filled by more adults and non school leavers. The drop in numbers comes in the face of the Howard Government's reduced funding to higher education. Page A1.

In the aftermath of the successful rescue of two yachtsmen from off the coast of Western Australia, Melbourne will lose its role in aviation rescue after allegations of bungling the rescue of one of the men, Thierry Dubois. All sea and land operations are to be co-ordinated from Canberra under the name of the Australian Maritime Safety Authority. Page A2.

Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett has left open the possibility of more privately operated hospital emergency departments if hospital networks could not provide enough doctors for 24-hour emergency care. Page A3.

After protests surrounding the environmental impact of an oil terminal at Crib Point, Shell International has backed down and deferred the project "indefinitely". The company's environmental adviser Dr Peter Langcake said Shell will hold off building the erminal for as long as strong opposition remains. Page A3.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
